comparison.summary: These three supplied solutions model repeated purchases directly. The existing catalog solution separates one-time first purchases from a final allowance for globally cheapest extra copies. Both approaches maximize the same total item count.
details: Plain DFS and memoized DFS track the current type, remaining budget, and whether the next paid purchase of that type would be its first. A take stays at the current type and sets the flag to false; a skip moves to the next type and sets it to true.
The mixed-knapsack solution handles each type with a backward first-purchase pass and a forward additional-purchase pass. It returns dp[budget] directly instead of scanning leftover allowances.
Plain DFS repeats states and is intended for studying small cases. Memoized DFS and bottom-up DP both take O(N² + NB) time, where N is the number of types and B is the budget.
Memoization uses O(NB) saved states plus the recursive stack; bottom-up DP uses O(B) space. Each version includes matching JavaScript and Python explanations and a complete trace of the same example.

solutions.title: DFS without memoization
solutions.intuition: At each type, decide whether to stop buying it or buy one more copy. Its first paid copy adds its one-time gifts; every later copy adds only one item. Explore both choices and keep the larger total.
solutions.approach: Count the free rewards for each type. Start dfs at index 0 with the full budget and isRewardAvailable = true. Skip the current type by moving to the next index with isRewardAvailable = true. If it is affordable, also buy one copy: add 1 plus its rewards only when isRewardAvailable is true, subtract the price, and recurse at the same index with isRewardAvailable = false. Return the larger result. Stop with zero additional items when all types are processed or no money remains.
hints: What is different about the first paid copy of a type compared with its later paid copies?
Which flag tells you whether the current type’s one-time rewards are still available?
Skipping moves to the next type. Buying stays at the same type so another copy remains available.

pseudocode.concept: Skip the current type, or buy another copy and award its gifts only on its first paid purchase.
steps: Initialize every reward count to zero. Compare every pair of different types and count divisible factors.
Define dfs with the current index, remaining budget, and whether this type’s one-time rewards are still available.
If there are no types left or the remaining budget is zero, return zero.
Find the current price. Compute skip by calling the next index with the same budget and isRewardAvailable set to true.
If the price exceeds the remaining budget, return skip.
Set value to one paid copy. If isRewardAvailable is true, add its reward count.
Compute take by adding value to dfs at the same index with the price subtracted and isRewardAvailable set to false.
Return max(skip, take). Start with dfs(0, budget, true).

solutions.explanation:
1. For each type i, rewards[i] counts the other types j whose factor is divisible by items[i][0]. Excluding i keeps the paid copy separate: its value is always 1. A free copy never activates another gift round. Paying for different types can award multiple copies of the same gift type; those copies all count.

2. dfs(i, remaining, isRewardAvailable) returns the best additional item count available from type i onward. The flag is named isRewardAvailable in JavaScript and is_reward_available in Python. True means type i’s one-time rewards have not been claimed yet, so buying it adds rewards[i]. The flag can be true even when rewards[i] is zero. Receiving a free copy does not change this flag. Skip moves to i + 1 and sets the flag to true because the next type has not been bought in this branch. Take stays at i and sets the flag to false because its one-time rewards have now been claimed; later paid copies add no gifts.

3. Every possible paid-copy count for the current type is represented: skip immediately means zero copies; take once and then skip means one; further takes mean more copies. Budget decreases on every take, so the recursion ends. Comparing skip and take at every state covers every affordable combination.

4. The result returned by a child counts only future copies. Each caller adds the value of the copy it just bought. The flag belongs to the current type; resetting it after a skip prevents a previous type’s purchases from suppressing the new type’s gifts.

5. This version repeats identical states. It is useful for learning the choices on small examples, but its exponential running time is unsuitable for the largest inputs. The memoized version below saves those repeated answers.

6. Each edge either skips one type or pays at least the minimum price P. A path therefore has at most N + floor(B / P) + 1 calls. The Python version raises the recursion limit to cover that path, keeping a higher existing limit. This changes only the allowed call depth; it does not reduce the work.

solutions.title: Bottom-up DP (Mixed Knapsack)
solutions.intuition: Each type combines two knapsack rules: its first paid copy earns a one-time bonus, while additional paid copies are unlimited and each adds one item. Process the first copy backward through the budget, then process additional copies forward.
solutions.approach: Create dp[c] for the best item count affordable with at most c money. For each type, count its free rewards, excluding itself. Let firstPurchaseValue be 1 plus that reward. First visit capacities from budget down to price, adding this first-purchase value at most once. Then visit capacities from price up to budget, adding one item for each additional paid copy. After all types, return dp[budget].
hints: Treat the first copy and later copies of a type as two different values at the same price.
Which loop direction prevents a one-time bonus from being used again in the same pass?
Which loop direction lets the next capacity reuse a result that already bought an extra copy?

pseudocode.concept: For each type, use one backward 0/1 pass for its first purchase and one forward unbounded pass for extra copies.
steps: Initialize dp[0] through dp[budget] to zero.
For each type, read its factor and price. Count every other divisible type into reward.
Set firstPurchaseValue to one paid copy plus reward.
Visit c from budget down to price. Set dp[c] to max(dp[c], dp[c - price] + firstPurchaseValue).
Visit c from price up to budget. Set dp[c] to max(dp[c], dp[c - price] + 1).
After every type has been processed, return dp[budget].

solutions.explanation:
1. The first paid copy contributes 1 plus reward. reward counts only other divisible types, so the paid copy is counted exactly once. Free copies do not trigger new gift rounds.

2. Before processing a type, dp[c] is the best count using earlier types with at most c money. The backward pass reads dp[c - price] before that smaller capacity has been updated for this type. Therefore the current type’s first-purchase bonus is used at most once.

3. After that pass, every capacity can already use zero or one paid copy of the current type. The forward pass can read a smaller capacity updated earlier in the same pass. It extends that purchase by another copy worth 1, allowing unlimited extra copies without awarding more gifts.

4. A forward candidate might be based on a state that has no copy of the current type. Counting its new copy as only 1 would undercount its first-purchase gifts, not overcount them. The backward pass already offered that same first copy with its full value of 1 + reward, which is at least 1. Thus those undercounted candidates cannot hide the better first-purchase choice.

5. For any affordable positive number of current copies, the backward pass accounts for the first copy and the forward pass can add all remaining copies. Keeping the old dp[c] also covers buying zero copies. These possibilities cover every paid-copy count, and maximizing them preserves the DP meaning after each type.

6. Capacity means an upper allowance, not an exact amount that must be spent. dp starts at zero because buying nothing is always allowed. Return dp[budget] directly; there is no final scan for cheapest copies.

solutions.title: DFS with memoization
solutions.intuition: Keep the same skip-or-buy decisions, but save their answer. If two purchase paths reach the same type, remaining money, and reward availability flag, their future choices are identical.
solutions.approach: Precompute rewards exactly as in plain DFS. Use the three-part state (i, remaining, isRewardAvailable) as the memo key. Return a cached answer before exploring children. Otherwise compute skip with the next index and isRewardAvailable = true. When the price fits, compute take: add rewards only when isRewardAvailable is true, then stay at the same index with isRewardAvailable = false. Save the larger result under that key. Start at index 0 with the full budget and isRewardAvailable = true.
hints: Which values determine all future purchases and whether the current type still has its first-purchase gifts?
Two calls can share i and remaining but have different isRewardAvailable flags. Must their answers be the same?
Check the cache before exploring skip and take. A saved zero is a valid answer too.

pseudocode.concept: Memoize the skip-or-buy DFS by index, remaining budget, and reward availability flag.
steps: Count each type’s free rewards by checking every other type’s factor. Create an empty memo.
If all types are processed or remaining is zero, return zero.
Build a key from i, remaining, and isRewardAvailable. If it exists in memo, return its answer.
Read the price. Compute skip at the next index with the same remaining budget and isRewardAvailable set to true.
Initialize take to zero. If the price fits, start value at one and add rewards only when isRewardAvailable is true.
Compute take as value plus the same index with the price subtracted and isRewardAvailable set to false.
Store and return max(skip, take). Start with dfs(0, budget, true).

solutions.explanation:
1. For each type i, rewards[i] counts the other types j whose factor is divisible by items[i][0]. Excluding i keeps the paid copy separate: its value is always 1. A free copy never activates another gift round. Paying for different types can award multiple copies of the same gift type; those copies all count.

2. dfs(i, remaining, isRewardAvailable) returns the best additional item count available from type i onward. The flag is named isRewardAvailable in JavaScript and is_reward_available in Python. True means type i’s one-time rewards have not been claimed yet, so buying it adds rewards[i]. The flag can be true even when rewards[i] is zero. Receiving a free copy does not change this flag. Skip moves to i + 1 and sets the flag to true because the next type has not been bought in this branch. Take stays at i and sets the flag to false because its one-time rewards have now been claimed; later paid copies add no gifts.

3. The memo key must include isRewardAvailable. With the same index and remaining money, a type’s first copy may still include gifts in one state but not in another. JavaScript encodes the three values as a comma-separated string; Python uses a tuple.

4. A key-presence check distinguishes a cached zero from a missing answer. On a cache hit the function returns immediately. On a miss it computes the skip and affordable take branches once, stores the result, and returns it. The base case returns zero before making a key.

5. There are at most 2 × N × (B + 1) non-base states: two flag values for each index and remaining budget. Each state makes at most two child calls and constant extra work, using expected constant-time map or dictionary operations. Rewards take a separate N² scan.

6. Each edge either skips one type or pays at least the minimum price P. A path therefore has at most N + floor(B / P) + 1 calls. The Python version raises the recursion limit to cover that path, keeping a higher existing limit. This changes only the allowed call depth; it does not reduce the work.

timeComplexityBreakdown.variables: N is the number of item types. B is the total budget. Each state also has one of two isRewardAvailable values: true or false. P is the minimum price and is used in the stack-space bound.

phases.label: Compare every pair of types to count free rewards
Compute at most 2N(B + 1) states, with at most two child calls each

timeComplexityBreakdown.note: Memoization eliminates repeated state evaluation. These bounds use expected constant-time map or dictionary operations and the usual fixed-width integer model for the problem bounds. The boolean flag contributes a constant factor of two.

solutions.spaceComplexity: O(NB) memo + O(N + B/P) rewards and recursion stack

variables.N: Number of item types in items.
variables.B: Total budget, measured in price units.
variables.P: Smallest item price in items; B / P bounds the number of paid copies.

notes: The reward availability flag describes the current type only; set it to true when moving to the next type. Receiving a free copy does not change the flag.
Memoization reduces repeated work, but recursive calls still need stack space. Bottom-up DP uses O(B) space.
